items.title: Compose reusable workflows
items.text:
Wrap high-level operations in application functions when a workflow needs several steps. Keep connection ownership with the caller and let failures propagate so the caller can handle them. The following function creates a new address and group; both names must be unused.

from pyfortinet import FMG
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address, AddressGroup


def create_backend_group(fmg: FMG, name: str, subnet: str) -> AddressGroup:
    address = Address(name=f"{name}-address", subnet=subnet)
    fmg.add(address)
    group = fmg.get_obj(AddressGroup, name=name, member=[address])
    group.add()
    return group

Call this function inside an open synchronous connection. These writes are separate operations: if group creation fails, the address may remain. Define cleanup or reconciliation for your application. Subclassing FMG is also possible, but custom synchronous methods are not converted to async methods by using an asynchronous context.

items.title: Choosing sync or async context management
items.text:
FMG supports both connection context protocols. Use the imports and config from the quickstart:

with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    addresses = fmg.get(Address).data

async def read_addresses():
    async with FMG(**config) as fmg:
        return (await fmg.get(Address)).data

Each async entry creates a separate AsyncFMG client with async methods and response types. Objects fetched or bound with fmg.get_obj(...) inside that context use this async client as well. Use the value bound by as fmg for operations; the original manager retains its synchronous API.

A manager can be reused sequentially in either mode. Its configuration is shared with the yielded async client, so changes to properties such as adom and raise_on_error persist between contexts. Overlapping async contexts or mixing an open sync connection with an async context on the same manager raise FMGConfigurationException. Separate managers can be used independently.

FMG.open() and FMG.close() remain synchronous. Use AsyncFMG for manual await client.open() and await client.close() management. Async context cleanup preserves the existing discard-on-error behavior and propagates exceptions. Custom synchronous subclass methods are not converted to async methods.

items.title: Explicit workspace locking
items.text:
Use with fmg.lock_adom("root"): for synchronous operations and async with fmg.lock_adom("root"): for asynchronous operations. The context releases locks it acquired, including when the operation raises an exception. Existing locks are preserved; keep_locked=True also preserves a newly acquired lock. Unlocking a selected ADOM leaves other ADOM locks intact. lock_adoms() and unlock_adoms() return successful responses only when all requested operations succeed, and their data includes a result for each ADOM. Workspace mode discovery raises FMGLockException when its reply is unsuccessful or incomplete and leaves the cached mode unset.

Discovery uses the global workspace setting unless it is per-adom. In that case it reads workspace_mode from /dvmdb/adom/{adom} for the requested ADOM. Each explicit locking context refreshes discovery, so switching ADOMs cannot reuse another ADOM's setting. Calling fmg.lock() without arguments uses the selected ADOM (or root when none is selected); with multiple ADOMs, only those with workspace enabled are locked. Normal and workflow modes both require locking; this does not create workflow sessions. Closing the client still cleans up retained locks even if the last ADOM checked has workspace disabled.

The Global Database does not use a workspace when global mode is per-adom, so automatic locking skips global in that mode. Under global normal and workflow, it requires locking. See the developer verification notes for the recorded FMG 7.4.6 checks and firmware limitations.

items.title: Selecting fields and scopes
items.text: High-level get calls accept fields=["name", ...] to request selected fields. Returned objects retain the scope used by the request, so their later operations continue to target that scope even when the client's selected ADOM changes. An object's explicit scope takes precedence over the request's scope. Successful high-level GET replies with absent or null data return an empty object list.

items.title: Device system configuration schemas
items.text:
DeviceInterface covers all 285 interface attributes in the supplied FortiManager 7.6.7 Configuration Database v7.4 Device Level Config schema, including mediatype. It accepts both Python names such as snmp_index and API names such as snmp-index, and writes API aliases. IPv6 settings, DHCP client options, secondary IP entries, tagging, and VRRP accept nested dictionaries and preserve their documented structure. Existing secondary-IP address shorthand remains supported. dns_server_protocol accepts either a single protocol string or an array from FMG and normalizes it to a list, preserving the schema's array shape when serialized.

The reference uses the same interface object definition for GET responses and ADD/SET/UPDATE inputs and does not mark attributes read-only. Fields therefore remain optional, with no device defaults injected into writes; a partial GET response does not need every configuration attribute. device and fmg_interface locate the object and are excluded from its configuration payload. The interface's API identity is name; interface is a separate parent-interface reference. GET replies retain URL-only parent parameters from the request, including device and a zone's vdom, so returned objects can be updated or refreshed without supplying those parameters again. Request filters and terminal object selectors are not copied into returned configuration data. Platform-specific availability still depends on the managed FortiGate. The schema targets FortiOS 7.4 on FMG 7.6.7; it is not evidence that every attribute exists on every 7.4 device or older FMG.

SystemAdmin also covers the reference's old-password input (old_password in Python). Administrator VDOM references serialize as name arrays. DeviceZone.tagging accepts structured category/name/tag rows, while its response metadata oid is excluded from writes because it is not a configuration attribute in the reference. Existing attributes for older firmware remain available even when they are absent from this particular schema.

items.title: Waiting for tasks
items.text:
Task polling works with FMGBase and AsyncFMGBase as well as the high-level clients.

Both clients accept task responses containing either taskid or task and retry transient connection failures until the polling timeout. Async callbacks may be functions or callable objects returning an awaitable. Failed task-creation responses and replies without task metadata are not polled; waiting returns None. When a status read returns a failed response, waiting also returns None without invoking the progress callback. Tasks completed with warnings return "warning"; callers can distinguish this from "done" and "error".

During asynchronous polling, keep synchronous callbacks brief: long-running callbacks block the event loop and delay other coroutines. For callbacks that perform I/O, use an asynchronous function and await nonblocking operations.

items.title: Using callbacks while waiting
items.text:
To display the current completion percentage and latest log line:

state = fmg.wait_for_task(task_id, callback=lambda percent, log: print(percent, log))

For a progress bar, install the optional Rich dependency with pyfortinet[rich] or pyfortinet[all]. This synchronous example uses the config from the quickstart and installs device settings onto the selected firewall. Review pending configuration before running it, and replace branch-fw with the intended device name.

from rich.progress import Progress

from pyfortinet import FMG
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.securityconsole import InstallDeviceTask

firewall = "branch-fw"
with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    task = fmg.get_obj(
        InstallDeviceTask,
        adom=fmg.adom,
        scope=[Scope(name=firewall, vdom="root")],
        flags=["auto_lock_ws"],
    )
    result = task.exec()
    with Progress() as progress:
        prog_task = progress.add_task(f"Installing settings on {firewall}", total=100)
        state = result.wait_for_task(
            callback=lambda percent, log: progress.update(prog_task, completed=percent)
        )
    if state != "done":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Installation did not complete successfully: {state}")

items.title: Connection cleanup
items.text:
Malformed login replies and missing session tokens raise FMGTokenException in both clients.

Calling open() on an already open client keeps the existing session and workspace locks. To start a new session, close the client first.

close() is safe before opening a connection and after it has already been closed. Both clients release the HTTP session and clear authentication and cached workspace state even if logout fails. For async clients, await close().

Workspace commit and unlock failures are logged and raised after logout and session cleanup. A failed commit response raises FMGLockException, including when raise_on_error=False, because there is no response object returned from close() for the caller to inspect. Unlock is still attempted when a commit fails. If a with or async with block is already exiting with an exception, cleanup failures are logged and the original exception continues to propagate. On normal exit, cleanup errors are raised.

close(discard_changes=True) applies only to that close operation. It leaves the configured discard_on_close setting unchanged when the client is opened again.

items.title: Batch write validation
items.text: Write batches must be nonempty and contain either only request dictionaries or only API objects. Low-level clients accept dictionaries only. Invalid batches raise FMGWrongRequestException, or return a failed response when raise_on_error=False, before contacting FortiManager.

items.title: Invalid API replies
items.text: Malformed JSON-RPC replies, including empty result lists and missing status codes, raise FMGUnhandledException. With raise_on_error=False, calls return a failed response instead. Successful GET results may still contain absent or null data; the result envelope must include a valid status code.

items.title: Filtering with F
items.text:
F builds the filter argument for high-level FMG.get() and AsyncFMG.get() calls. The same expressions work with both clients; only the request needs awaiting. Import the resource class and use an open connection configured as in the quickstart:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import F
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address

filters = F(name__like="server%") & F(type="ipmask")
addresses = fmg.get(Address, filters=filters).data

Filters are sent to FortiManager, which evaluates them against the selected table. Local construction checks the operator syntax; it does not validate field names or establish that a particular firmware supports an operator for that field.

items.title: One condition and comparison operators
items.text:
Use F(field=value) for equality or F(field__operator=value) for an explicit comparison. Each F accepts one condition. Combine separate instances for multiple conditions.

Suffix API operator Example omitted or eq == F(name="server1") neq != F(type__neq="fqdn") lt, le <, <= F(color__lt=10) gt, ge >, >= F(color__ge=2) in in F(name__in=["server1", "server2"]) contain contain F(member__contain="server1") like, not_like like, !like F(name__like="server%") glob, not_glob glob, !glob F(name__glob="server*") or & (bitwise test) F(flags__or=[3, 1])

in compares a field with several candidate values; contain searches a list-valued field for a member. Choose a resource that exposes the field: for example, member belongs to an address group rather than an address.

The legacy suffix __or maps to the API's bitwise &, not logical OR. The implementation comments describe one integer target as testing (source & target) == 0, and two targets as testing (source & mask) == expected. Verify the field and semantics against your firmware reference before using it. Use | between conditions for logical OR.

Unknown suffixes and multiple conditions in one F raise ValueError. Values retain their Python types; a list expands into separate API targets:

assert F(name="server1").generate() == ["name", "==", "server1"]
assert F(name__in=["server1", "server2"]).generate() == [
    "name", "in", "server1", "server2"
]
assert F(color__ge=2).generate() == ["color", ">=", 2]

items.title: API field names and separators
items.text:
F does not look up a model's aliases. Its default _sep="_" preserves underscores. For API fields with dashes, set _sep="-"; a leading underscore is preserved:

assert F(allow_routing="enable").generate() == ["allow_routing", "==", "enable"]
assert F(allow_routing="enable", _sep="-").generate() == ["allow-routing", "==", "enable"]
assert F(_image_base64__like="data%", _sep="-").generate() == [
    "_image-base64", "like", "data%"
]

For fields containing spaces or other characters that cannot appear in Python keyword names, pass the exact API name through a dictionary:

assert F(**{"scope member__in": ["branch-fw"]}).generate() == [
    "scope member", "in", "branch-fw"
]

Use the endpoint's actual API spelling. For example, device inventory fields such as conn_status retain underscores.

items.title: AND, OR, and implicit OR lists
items.text:
Use & for AND, | for explicit OR, and + for the API's implicit OR list. Python and and or do not build filter expressions.

assert (F(name="server1") | F(name="server2")).generate() == [
    ["name", "==", "server1"], "||", ["name", "==", "server2"]
]
assert (F(name="server1") + F(name="server2")).generate() == [
    ["name", "==", "server1"], ["name", "==", "server2"]
]

filters = (F(name="server1") | F(name="server2")) & F(type="ipmask")
assert filters.generate() == [
    [["name", "==", "server1"], "||", ["name", "==", "server2"]],
    "&&",
    ["type", "==", "ipmask"],
]

Parenthesize mixed expressions: Python evaluates + before &, and & before |. Parentheses around adjacent expressions with the same operator may disappear because the builder flattens those lists. Different operators retain their nested structure.

A tricky case from the tests combines protocol conditions with a null-or-zero check:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ServiceCustom

filters = (F(protocol="ICMP") & F(icmptype="8")) & (F(icmpcode=None) + F(icmpcode=0))
assert filters.generate() == [
    [["protocol", "==", "ICMP"], "&&", ["icmptype", "==", "8"]],
    "&&",
    [["icmpcode", "==", None], ["icmpcode", "==", 0]],
]
services = fmg.get(ServiceCustom, filters).data

Here None remains an explicit filter target; it is not omitted like a null field in a write payload. FortiManager decides whether a null comparison is meaningful for the selected field.

items.title: Negation and reusable conditions
items.text:
~F(...) negates one condition and returns a copy. Inverting it again removes the negation:

online = F(conn_status="up")
offline = ~online
assert online.generate() == ["conn_status", "==", "up"]
assert offline.generate() == ["!", "conn_status", "==", "up"]
assert (~offline).generate() == online.generate()

Negation is implemented for individual F instances, not combined filter groups. To express NOT (A OR B), negate both conditions and join them with AND:

filters = ~F(name="server1") & ~F(name="server2")

Use ~, not Python not, which produces a boolean. Composition preserves existing expressions, so you can reuse a base condition without altering it.

items.title: Build a filter dynamically
items.text:
An empty F() can seed a nonempty sequence on the left of |, &, or +. Handle an empty input explicitly rather than generating or sending the empty seed:

hosts = ["server1", "server2"]
if not hosts:
    addresses = []  # No requested names means no lookup in this application.
else:
    filters = F()
    for host in hosts:
        filters |= F(name=host)
    addresses = fmg.get(Address, filters).data

Do not use the truth value of F() to test whether any conditions were added. Track the input or accumulated conditions explicitly.

items.title: Text filters
items.text:
High-level GET also accepts a text expression. Use the suffix names from the operator table, such as eq and like, with lowercase and, or, or a comma for implicit OR. Use text_to_filter() to inspect the generated structure without a connection:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import text_to_filter

expression = "(name eq server1 or name eq server2) and type eq ipmask"
filters = text_to_filter(expression)
assert filters.generate() == (
    (F(name="server1") | F(name="server2")) & F(type="ipmask")
).generate()
addresses = fmg.get(Address, expression).data

assert text_to_filter("~name like host_%").generate() == ["!", "name", "like", "host_%"]
assert text_to_filter("name eq server1, name eq server2").generate() == [
    ["name", "==", "server1"], ["name", "==", "server2"]
]

The parser is deliberately small. Values are single non-whitespace tokens and remain strings; it does not implement quoted values with spaces, Python lists, or numeric conversion. Prefer F(comment="Application server"), F(color__ge=2), and F(name__in=[...]) for those cases.

Mixed unparenthesized text is parsed recursively from the right, rather than following Python's operator precedence. For example, name eq server1 and type eq ipmask or type eq fqdn groups as name eq server1 and (type eq ipmask or type eq fqdn). Always use explicit parentheses when mixing operators. Malformed expressions raise ValueError.

items.title: Patterns and inspection
items.text:
The operator comments describe SQL-style like patterns: % matches any sequence of characters and _ matches a single character. Thus host_% does not mean a literal underscore. glob uses case-sensitive Unix-style patterns, such as host-*. Use equality for a literal name containing wildcard characters.

Call .generate() to inspect grouping, field spelling, and value types. It only builds a local list and makes no request. The examples above follow the offline common/filter composition tests; endpoint-specific matching still requires a compatible FortiManager.

items.title: Custom service port ranges
items.text:
For a single port, PortRange accepts either the start or end endpoint. For example, PortRange(destination_start="443") and PortRange(destination_end="443") both serialize to 443.

Service port-range lists can mix strings and PortRange objects in either order. Invalid entries raise a Pydantic ValidationError instead of being silently omitted. Explicit None values remain unset.

items.title: Optional collection serialization
items.text: Optional member, category, and port-range collections preserve None during model serialization. Explicit empty lists remain empty lists, allowing them to clear an existing collection.

items.title: Response lookup
items.text: A low-level response containing one dictionary supports response[0] and response["object-name", "name"], like a response containing a list of result dictionaries. For API objects without declared master keys, supply the lookup field explicitly.

items.title: Refresh failures
items.text: refresh() requires a successful lookup of exactly one object. A failed lookup leaves the object unchanged and raises a library exception, including when raise_on_error=False; no refreshed object can be returned in that case.

items.title: Transport retries and timeouts
items.text:
Both clients use pyresilience for transport retries. JSON-RPC get operations retry connection failures, native timeouts, and HTTP status codes 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504. The decision uses the JSON-RPC method: every FMG request uses HTTP POST.

Login, logout, writes, and exec operations have one transport attempt. Replaying them after losing a response could duplicate a completed operation. Existing authentication renewal and workspace-lock recovery still handle explicit API rejections separately. API validation errors, malformed JSON, certificate failures, and other HTTP errors are not retried.

Configure the same settings on FMGSettings, FMG, FMGBase, or their async counterparts:

Setting Default Meaning retry_attempts 3 Total attempts per read request, including the first retry_delay 0.1 Initial backoff in seconds retry_backoff 2.0 Backoff multiplier retry_max_delay 2.0 Backoff cap in seconds retry_jitter True Randomize backoff delays timeout 120.0 Native connect/read inactivity timeout in seconds

Set retry_attempts=1 to disable automatic transport retries. Exhausted transport failures retain their native requests/aiohttp exception types. HTTP errors raise FMGHTTPException, whose status_code attribute identifies the HTTP status. For JSON-RPC operations, raise_on_error=False converts this to a failed response.

timeout applies to each attempt's connection and read inactivity limits, including response-body reading. Multiple attempts and backoff can increase total elapsed time. It is not a strict overall wall-clock deadline. The async transport uses the corresponding aiohttp.ClientTimeout connection and socket limits rather than aiohttp's separate total-request timer.

The override works with both clients and validates positive, finite timeout values. Async overrides are local to the current task's context, so overlapping tasks can use different values on the same client. Nested blocks restore the previous override on exit, including when an exception occurs:

with fmg.timeout(30):
    response = fmg.get(Address)

# When fmg is an AsyncFMG instance:
with fmg.timeout(30):
    response = await fmg.get(Address)

Sync requests stay on the caller's thread. pyresilience's thread-based sync timeout wrapper is not used because it cannot reliably interrupt blocking socket I/O; see its timeout implementation notes. Async cancellation propagates immediately. Each response is released before retrying or returning.

items.title: From FortiManager API calls to Python objects
items.text:
If you already use How to FortiManager API, the underlying concepts remain familiar: ADOMs, configuration objects, policy packages, workspace locks, and asynchronous tasks. pyfortinet represents supported resources as Python models and handles request construction, authentication, and response conversion.

The external guide explains the JSON-RPC API and covers more endpoints than pyfortinet currently models. Use it for API context and Fortinet's firmware-specific reference for field and route definitions. Use this guide for workflows built with the implemented high-level classes.

items.title: Translate operations into object methods
items.text: API concept High-level Python API Login, session token, logout with FMG(**config) as fmg: ADOM portion of an object URL adom in connection settings or an explicit object scope GET an object table fmg.get(Address).data Select an address by name fmg.get(Address(name="server1")).first() Filter expressions F(...) combined with &, \|, and ~ ADD a configuration object fmg.add(Address(name="server1", subnet="192.0.2.1/32")) UPDATE selected fields fmg.update(Address(name="server1", comment="Application server")) DELETE an identified object fmg.delete(Address(name="server1")) Device-specific override A model's dynamic_mapping and Scope Execute an operation fmg.exec(task) or a bound task's .exec() Poll a returned task ID response.wait_for_task()

items.title: Models, bound objects, and responses
items.text:
Address(...) creates a local Pydantic model. It validates supported fields but makes no API call. fmg.get_obj(Address, name="server1") constructs a model bound to a client, also without an API call. Binding an existing instance with fmg.get_obj(address) returns that same instance. Neither operation fetches the object's configuration.

Call fmg.get(...) to read configuration. High-level GET responses contain typed models in .data; the returned models are bound to the requesting client. This enables methods such as .refresh(), .update(), and .delete(). With an asynchronous client, await these methods.

.success and the response's truth value describe request success. They do not indicate whether a GET found an object: a successful empty lookup has .data == [] and .first() is None. Write and execution responses do not necessarily contain a typed object. Read or refresh the object when you need FortiManager's resulting configuration.

items.title: Scope and policy packages
items.text:
Choose an ADOM explicitly when connecting. The settings default is global, which refers to the Global Database. An explicit object's fmg_scope takes precedence over the connection's selected ADOM. Fetched objects retain their request scope even if fmg.adom later changes.

Policy objects also require a policy package, abbreviated PP. Inside an open connection, read the policies in an existing package:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.policy import Policy

policies = fmg.get(Policy(pkg="branch-policy")).data
for policy in policies:
    print(policy.policyid, policy.name)

Replace branch-policy with a package in your selected ADOM. The model constructs its URL; you do not need to assemble a /pm/config/... path.

items.title: Write, commit, and install are separate steps
items.text:
An object write changes FortiManager's database. With workspace enabled, the client can acquire ADOM locks in response to a lock-required API error. Explicit locking is also available. Normal connection cleanup attempts to commit workspaces locked by that client and release locks. discard_on_close=True skips those commits; discard_on_error=True is the default when an exception leaves the context. Neither setting reverses an installation or every device operation.

An installation task applies configuration to selected managed devices. Its successful creation does not establish that installation has completed. Keep the connection open, wait for the task, and check its terminal state. See the installation how-to.

items.title: Coverage and extension
items.text:
The object guides organize supported models by domain. The generated code reference describes their complete field lists. Model validation does not guarantee that every firmware or device platform accepts every field. _version metadata does not enforce firmware compatibility.

When a resource has no model, low-level clients and dictionary requests remain available. For reusable workflows, consider contributing a model using the API object implementation guide, so callers can continue working with Python objects.

items.title: Firewall objects
items.text:
This guide covers every public class exported by pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall, grouped by purpose. Resource models support high-level operations; helper models are embedded in resource fields and are not added independently.

Run request examples inside an open connection from the quickstart. Examples with fmg.add(...) or fmg.update(...) write to the selected ADOM; await those calls with an asynchronous client. Constructing a model makes no API request and installs no configuration. Examples in each family build on their preceding snippets. Use unused resource names, and replace device names, interfaces, profile references, and tagging categories with values in your ADOM.

Family Public classes Addresses Address, AddressGroup, AddressTagging Services ServiceCategory, ServiceCustom, PortRange, ServiceGroup Security profiles ProfileGroup Proxy objects ProxyAddress, ProxyAddressGroup, ProxyAddressHeaderGroup Proxy metadata ProxyAddressTagging, ProxyAddressGroupTagging Internet services InternetService Virtual IPs VIP, VIPDynamicMapping IP pools IPPool, IPPoolDynamicMapping, IPPoolGroup Shared mapping helper Scope

Python field names generally use underscores; serializers write the declared API aliases. Client writes omit None but retain explicit empty lists. Consult the class reference for defaults that may also be serialized, particularly when making a partial update.

items.title: Firmware coverage
items.text:
The proxy, Internet service, VIP, and IP pool models follow the supplied FortiManager 7.6.7 Configuration Database v7.4 ADOM Level Objects schema. This does not establish the firmware coverage of every older address, service, or profile field.

The existing verification record reports live FMG 7.4.6 build 2588 checks for five writable schema-backed resource types and VIP/IPPool mappings. InternetService lookups were skipped because the lab catalog was empty. FMG 7.6.7 device compatibility remains unverified. See the testing guide. The examples on this page are checked locally; they were not executed against a live device as part of this documentation update.

items.title: Choose an object family
items.text:
• Addresses and groups
  • Services
  • Security profiles
  • Proxy objects
  • Internet services
  • Virtual IPs
  • IP pools
  • Mapping scopes

items.title: How-tos
items.text: These examples use the imports and config from the quickstart. Unless a connection context is shown, run the snippet inside with FMG(**config) as fmg:. Replace example names with resources in your selected ADOM. Write examples modify FortiManager; installation examples also modify the selected FortiGate.

items.title: Find and filter objects
items.text:
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import F
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmdb import Device
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address

servers = fmg.get(Address, F(name__like="server%"), fields=["name", "subnet"]).data
offline = fmg.get(Device, F(name__like="branch-%") & ~F(conn_status="up")).data
either = fmg.get(Address, F(name="server1") | F(name="server2")).data

Use parentheses to make grouping explicit. & combines conditions with AND, | with OR, and ~ negates a condition. + creates the API's implicit OR list. An initialized model can also select an object: fmg.get(Address(name="server1")).first(). Always handle None before accessing the result of .first().

items.title: Create and bind objects
items.text:
address = Address(name="example-server", subnet="192.0.2.10/32")
fmg.add(address)

bound = fmg.get_obj(Address, name="example-backend", subnet="192.0.2.20/32")
bound.add()

Constructing or binding a model does not contact FortiManager. Both fmg.add(address) and bound.add() submit an ADD request. Use names that do not already exist.

items.title: Update, refresh, and delete
items.text:
server = fmg.get(Address(name="example-server")).first()
if server is None:
    raise LookupError("example-server does not exist")

fmg.update(Address(name=server.name, comment="Managed by the application"))
server.refresh()
print(server.comment)

To delete that address after removing any references to it:

server.delete()

refresh() reloads a bound object in place and requires exactly one match. update() sends the model's non-null fields; using a small model limits the fields sent. None is omitted from high-level write payloads. An explicit empty list is sent and can clear a collection.

items.title: Create an address group
items.text:
Create member addresses before the group that references them:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import AddressGroup

backend = Address(name="example-group-backend", subnet="192.0.2.30/32")
fmg.add(backend)
group = AddressGroup(name="example-backends", member=[backend])
fmg.add(group)

Members may be object instances or names; the serializer sends their names. Supplying a member object does not create it automatically. When removing these resources, delete the group first.

items.title: Add or remove a device-specific address mapping
items.text:
The address and device must already exist. Select the device explicitly:

server = fmg.get(Address(name="example-server")).first()
device = fmg.get(Device(name="branch-fw")).first()
if server is None or device is None:
    raise LookupError("The example address and branch-fw device must already exist")

mapping = Address(
    mapping__scope=device.get_vdom_scope("root"),
    subnet="198.51.100.10/32",
)
# This example replaces the complete mapping collection with one override.
fmg.update(Address(name=server.name, dynamic_mapping=[mapping]))
server.refresh()
print(server.dynamic_mapping)

Use the target device's actual VDOM. Preserve existing mapping entries if they must remain. To remove all overrides from this address:

fmg.update(Address(name=server.name, dynamic_mapping=[]))
server.refresh()

Mappings are embedded in the address payload. A GET returns a response; use .first() to obtain the address before accessing its attributes.

items.title: Work with workspace locks
items.text:
Automatic locking handles lock-required API replies. To hold a lock across a known operation:

with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    with fmg.lock_adom(fmg.adom):
        fmg.update(Address(name="example-server", comment="Reviewed configuration"))
        fmg.lock.commit_changes([fmg.adom])

Commit before leaving an explicit lock context when changes should be saved. The context releases a lock it acquired; it preserves an existing lock or a lock requested with keep_locked=True. Normal connection cleanup attempts to commit locks still held by the client. Set discard_on_close=True to skip that commit. Workspace settings apply only where workspace is enabled and do not undo installations or provide a transaction across all operations.

For async clients, use async with fmg.lock_adom(...) and await requests and fmg.lock.commit_changes(...). Workflow session creation and approval are not automated. See advanced usage for scope rules.

items.title: Install device settings and wait for completion
items.text:
This operation installs device settings onto the explicitly named FortiGate. Review pending configuration first; installation can include changes made outside this script. Use an existing device and VDOM in the selected ADOM.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.securityconsole import InstallDeviceTask

with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    task = fmg.get_obj(
        InstallDeviceTask,
        adom=fmg.adom,
        scope=[Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")],
        flags=["auto_lock_ws"],
    )
    response = task.exec()
    state = response.wait_for_task(
        callback=lambda percent, log: print(f"Task at {percent}%: {log}")
    )
    if state != "done":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Installation did not complete successfully: {state}")

Keep the connection open while waiting. A successful execution response means the request was accepted; check the task state separately. Not every execution response contains a task ID. wait_for_task() returns None when there is no task to poll or a task-status request fails.

For an async client, use response = await task.exec() and state = await response.wait_for_task().

items.title: Handle request failures
items.text:
By default, library API failures raise exceptions. Handle the specific exception appropriate to your workflow, or catch FMGException at an application boundary:

from pyfortinet.exceptions import FMGException

try:
    with FMG(**config) as fmg:
        addresses = fmg.get(Address).data
except FMGException:
    print("The FortiManager request failed")

With raise_on_error=False, decorated JSON-RPC operations return failed responses for library exceptions; check response.success before using data. This setting does not suppress every Python, validation, transport, or refresh error. See advanced usage for transport exceptions.

items.title: Installation
items.text: pyfortinet requires Python 3.9 or later and Pydantic 2. Use a virtual environment to keep its dependencies separate from other applications.

items.title: Install with uv
items.text:
Install uv first if it is not already available. For an application that uses pyfortinet, create a project and add the dependency:

uv init fortimanager-automation
cd fortimanager-automation
uv add pyfortinet

For asynchronous support, use this dependency instead:

uv add "pyfortinet[async]"

Save an example as main.py and run it in the project environment:

uv run python main.py

uv manages the project's virtual environment and dependency lockfile. Activation is unnecessary when using uv run. See the uv project guide for details.

items.title: Use uv with a standalone virtual environment
items.text:
For a script directory without a uv project, use the uv pip interface:

uv venv
uv pip install "pyfortinet[all]"

Activate .venv using the platform-specific commands in the pip section below, then run your script with python main.py. uv pip install installs into the discovered environment; it does not add a dependency to pyproject.toml or maintain a project lockfile.

items.title: Work on pyfortinet itself
items.text:
For this repository, use its checked-in dependency resolution instead of creating a new project:

git clone https://github.com/realvitya/pyfortinet.git
cd pyfortinet
uv sync --locked
uv run invoke docs-serve

The default development group includes optional client dependencies and, on Python 3.11+, the Zensical documentation tools. Building or previewing docs requires Python 3.11+; using the library still requires only Python 3.9+. For a runtime-only source environment, use uv sync --locked --no-dev, adding --extra async, --extra rich, or --extra all as needed. See the developer guide for contribution checks.

items.title: Install with pip
items.text:
python -m venv .venv

Activate it on Linux or macOS:

source .venv/bin/activate

Or in Windows PowerShell:

.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Then install the package:

python -m pip install pyfortinet
Installation Includes pyfortinet Synchronous clients and object models pyfortinet[async] Adds aiohttp for asynchronous clients pyfortinet[rich] Adds Rich for optional formatted output pyfortinet[all] Adds both optional dependencies

Quote extras when installing from a shell:

python -m pip install "pyfortinet[async]"

items.title: Connect to FortiManager
items.text:
Use the FortiManager HTTPS URL, an account with JSON-RPC API access, and an explicit ADOM. The client appends /jsonrpc if absent from base_url. Username/password authentication is currently supported. Direct FortiGate connections are not implemented.

Certificate verification defaults to True. For the synchronous requests transport, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE can identify a trusted CA bundle. That setting is specific to requests; do not assume it configures aiohttp. For asynchronous clients, ensure the certificate is trusted by the Python SSL environment. verify=False disables certificate verification and should be limited to environments where you explicitly intend that behavior.

The quickstart reads credentials from environment variables to avoid storing them in example code. See the generated FMGSettings reference for connection settings and advanced usage for timeout and retry behavior.

items.title: Install from source
items.text:
To try the current repository version:

python -m pip install git+https://github.com/realvitya/pyfortinet.git

Source installations may differ from a published release. For editable installations, dependency management with uv, and contribution checks, follow the developer guide.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: Use FMG to work with FortiManager objects in Python. This example reads firewall addresses; it does not change configuration. Python 3.9 or later is required.

items.title: Install and configure
items.text:
python -m pip install pyfortinet

Use a FortiManager account with JSON-RPC API access and permission to read the selected ADOM. Set FMG_URL, FMG_USERNAME, FMG_PASSWORD, and FMG_ADOM in your environment before running the example. These are example-specific variable names read explicitly by the code below.

import os

from pyfortinet import FMG
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import F
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address

config = {
    "base_url": os.environ["FMG_URL"],
    "username": os.environ["FMG_USERNAME"],
    "password": os.environ["FMG_PASSWORD"],
    "adom": os.environ["FMG_ADOM"],
}

with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    addresses = fmg.get(Address, F(name__like="server%"))
    for address in addresses.data:
        print(address.name, address.subnet)

    server = fmg.get(Address(name="server1")).first()
    if server is None:
        print("server1 was not found")
    else:
        print(server.name, server.subnet)

The context opens an authenticated session and closes it on exit. High-level GET responses contain typed models in .data. .first() returns an object or None when nothing matches. Request failures raise exceptions by default. TLS certificate verification is enabled by default.

items.title: Update an address
items.text:
The following example uses the same config and changes an existing address in the selected ADOM:

with FMG(**config) as fmg:
    server = fmg.get(Address(name="server1")).first()
    if server is None:
        raise LookupError("Create server1 before running this example")
    fmg.update(Address(name=server.name, subnet="192.0.2.0/24"))

A model containing only the fields to change avoids writing unrelated values from a previous GET. Fetched objects are also bound to their client, so server.update() is available after changing their fields. Keep object operations inside the connection context.

On normal exit, the client attempts to commit workspaces it has locked. This saves changes in FortiManager; installing configuration onto a FortiGate is a separate operation. Workspace discard is not a general rollback mechanism. See the how-tos.

items.title: Use the same API asynchronously
items.text:
Install pyfortinet[async], then use the same imports and config with an asynchronous context:

import asyncio


async def main():
    async with FMG(**config) as fmg:
        addresses = await fmg.get(Address)
        for address in addresses.data:
            print(address.name, address.subnet)


asyncio.run(main())

async with FMG(...) yields an AsyncFMG client. Await its requests and operations on bound objects. get_obj(...) only constructs or binds a local model and is not awaited. You can also import AsyncFMG directly for explicit asynchronous connection management.

Continue with API concepts and the task-oriented how-tos.

items.title: Addresses and groups
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: Address
items.text:
Address represents firewall addresses. Use subnet for an IP address or network, start_ip and end_ip for a range, or fqdn with type="fqdn" for a DNS name.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address

server = Address(name="example-server", subnet="192.0.2.10/32")
network = Address(name="example-network", subnet="192.0.2.0/24")
dns_name = Address(name="example-site", type="fqdn", fqdn="www.example.com")
ip_range = Address(
    name="example-range", type="iprange", start_ip="192.0.2.100", end_ip="192.0.2.110"
)
fmg.add([server, network, dns_name, ip_range])

For device-specific overrides, embed another Address with mapping__scope in dynamic_mapping. See mapping how-tos. An unnamed Address can represent a mapping row; it is not a separate address to add.

items.title: AddressGroup
items.text:
Members can be existing address/group names or named models. Model references serialize as names; constructing a member model does not create the member in FortiManager. This example uses the addresses created above:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import AddressGroup

group = AddressGroup(
    name="example-servers",
    member=[server, "example-range"],
    comment="Application servers",
)
fmg.add(group)

Remove a group before deleting addresses that it references. Use an explicit empty member list to clear membership. Groups also support exclude_member and embedded AddressGroup mappings; check the reference for fields accepted by the target firmware.

items.title: AddressTagging
items.text:
AddressTagging is embedded metadata, not an independently writable API resource. Its category is a string and tags are a list. The referenced category and tags must be valid in your ADOM.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address, AddressTagging

tagged = Address(
    name="example-tagged-server",
    subnet="192.0.2.40/32",
    tagging=[AddressTagging(name="business-role", category="Role", tags=["Backend"])],
)
fmg.add(tagged)

items.title: Internet services
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: InternetService
items.text:
InternetService models the Internet Service Database fields on firewall/internet-service. The supplied reference exposes only GET, SET, and UPDATE at the collection URL. It defines no ADD, DELETE, CLONE, item-by-ID URL, or dynamic mapping. Unsupported object operations raise FMGWrongRequestException before sending a request.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import InternetService

service = fmg.get(InternetService(id=65536)).first()  # id becomes a GET filter

An ID remains in SET/UPDATE data; it is not appended to the URL. Firmware decides which database attributes are editable; the reference does not mark individual fields read-only.

items.title: IP pools
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: IPPool
items.text: IPPool uses firewall/ippool. It supports the reference's overload, one-to-one, fixed-port-range, port-block-allocation, and CGN resource-allocation types. IP values and metadata variables remain strings; array inputs such as exclude_ip preserve the API's list shape.

items.title: IPPoolDynamicMapping
items.text:
Use IPPoolDynamicMapping for mapping-specific fields, including IPv6 source prefixes, client prefix length, session quotas, and privileged-port PBA settings. Scope and mapping-array handling match VIPDynamicMapping; mapping-only fields are not sent on the parent object.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import IPPool, IPPoolDynamicMapping

pool = IPPool(
    name="outbound", type="overload", startip="203.0.113.10", endip="203.0.113.19",
    dynamic_mapping=IPPoolDynamicMapping(
        mapping__scope=Scope(name="FG01", vdom="root"),
        startip="203.0.113.20", endip="203.0.113.29",
    ),
)
fmg.add(pool)

items.title: IPPoolGroup
items.text:
IPPoolGroup uses the schema's firewall/ippool_grp route, with an underscore. Members can be pool names or IPPool objects and serialize as names. Member pools must use type="cgn-resource-allocation", have the same attributes except their public/client ranges, and belong to only one pool group. FMG enforces these relationships; the CGN type and exclusive membership requirements were verified on FMG 7.4.6 build 2588. Cloning a populated group attempts to reuse its pools and is rejected by that firmware. The group itself has no dynamic mapping in this reference; mappings belong to its member pools.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import IPPool, IPPoolGroup

pool = IPPool(
    name="cgn-pool", type="cgn-resource-allocation", startip="203.0.113.10", endip="203.0.113.19",
)
fmg.add(pool)
group = IPPoolGroup(name="outbound-pools", member=[pool])
fmg.add(group)

items.title: Mapping scopes
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: Scope
items.text:
Scope identifies a managed device and, where applicable, its VDOM. It is shared by several API domains and re-exported by the firewall package for convenience. It is not a resource to add.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address

device_scope = Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")
mapping = Address(mapping__scope=device_scope, subnet="198.51.100.10/32")
override = Address(name="example-server", dynamic_mapping=[mapping])
fmg.update(override)

The device, VDOM, and parent address must already exist. This replaces the address's entire mapping list with the supplied override; preserve other entries if they must remain.

items.title: Security profiles
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: ProfileGroup
items.text:
ProfileGroup references existing security profiles by name. It does not create antivirus, web-filter, or other profiles. Replace the profile names below with profiles present in your ADOM.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ProfileGroup

profiles = ProfileGroup(
    name="example-security-profiles",
    av_profile="existing-antivirus",
    webfilter_profile="existing-webfilter",
    ips_sensor="existing-ips",
)
fmg.add(profiles)

items.title: Proxy objects
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: ProxyAddress
items.text:
The example-server address referenced below must already exist.

ProxyAddress uses firewall/proxy-address in the selected ADOM or global scope. It supports header-group and tagging rows, HTTP method/browser arrays, and named host-address references. Single array values are accepted and serialized as arrays; references can be names or named high-level objects. _image-base64 is exposed as image_base64 in Python.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address, ProxyAddress

address = ProxyAddress(
    name="example-proxy-site", type="host-regex", host_regex=r".*\.example\.com",
    host=Address(name="example-server"), case_sensitivity="disable",
)
fmg.add(address)

The reference defines no proxy-address dynamic mapping; none is added by this client.

items.title: ProxyAddressGroup
items.text:
ProxyAddressGroup uses firewall/proxy-addrgrp. Members can be names or named objects and serialize as name arrays. type accepts src or dst. An omitted member field leaves it out of a write; member=[] explicitly sends an empty array. Tagging rows are supported.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ProxyAddressGroup

group = ProxyAddressGroup(name="example-sites", type="dst", member=[address])
fmg.add(group)

The reference defines no proxy-address-group dynamic mapping.

items.title: ProxyAddressHeaderGroup
items.text:
These helper models are embedded in a ProxyAddress. Header rows express HTTP header matching; tagging rows refer to existing categories and tags. Unlike AddressTagging, proxy tagging categories use lists.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import (
    ProxyAddress,
    ProxyAddressHeaderGroup,
    ProxyAddressTagging,
)

header_address = ProxyAddress(
    name="example-header",
    type="header",
    header_group=[
        ProxyAddressHeaderGroup(
            id=1, header_name="X-Environment", header="production", case_sensitivity="disable"
        )
    ],
    tagging=[
        ProxyAddressTagging(name="business-role", category=["Role"], tags=["Backend"])
    ],
)
fmg.add(header_address)

items.title: ProxyAddressTagging
items.text:
ProxyAddressTagging adds category and tag references to a proxy address. The preceding example embeds it in the initial ADD. To replace the tags on an existing proxy address, use a partial update:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ProxyAddress, ProxyAddressTagging

fmg.update(ProxyAddress(
    name="example-header",
    tagging=[ProxyAddressTagging(name="business-role", category=["Role"], tags=["Frontend"])],
))

This sends the complete replacement tagging list. The category and tags must already be available.

items.title: ProxyAddressGroupTagging
items.text:
Use ProxyAddressGroupTagging for metadata embedded in a proxy group. Member proxy addresses, categories, and tags must already exist:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ProxyAddressGroup, ProxyAddressGroupTagging

tagged_group = ProxyAddressGroup(
    name="example-tagged-sites",
    type="dst",
    member=["example-proxy-site"],
    tagging=[
        ProxyAddressGroupTagging(name="business-role", category=["Role"], tags=["Backend"])
    ],
)
fmg.add(tagged_group)

items.title: Services
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: ServiceCategory
items.text:
Create categories before custom services that reference them:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ServiceCategory

category = ServiceCategory(name="Example applications", comment="Application service definitions")
fmg.add(category)

items.title: ServiceCustom
items.text:
ServiceCustom models TCP, UDP, SCTP, ICMP, and other supported service definitions. Categories can be names or ServiceCategory instances. The category in this example was created above.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ServiceCustom

web = ServiceCustom(
    name="example-web",
    protocol="TCP/UDP/SCTP",
    category=[category],
    tcp_portrange=["443", "8443"],
)
dns = ServiceCustom(
    name="example-dns",
    protocol="TCP/UDP/SCTP",
    udp_portrange="53",
)
ping = ServiceCustom(name="example-ping", protocol="ICMP", icmptype=8, icmpcode=0)
fmg.add([web, dns, ping])

items.title: PortRange
items.text:
PortRange is a local helper for service port fields. It is serialized through ServiceCustom; do not pass it to fmg.add(). Strings use destination ports first, followed by optional source ports after a colon: destination-start-destination-end:source-start-source-end.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import PortRange, ServiceCustom

restricted = ServiceCustom(
    name="example-restricted-web",
    tcp_portrange=[
        "443",
        PortRange(
            destination_start="8443", destination_end="8444",
            source_start="1024", source_end="65535",
        ),
    ],
)
assert restricted.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)["tcp-portrange"] == [
    "443", "8443-8444:1024-65535"
]
fmg.add(restricted)

A single port accepts either endpoint: PortRange(destination_end="443") serializes to 443 when used in a service. Start values greater than end values raise a validation error. String and model entries may be mixed in either order; invalid entries are rejected.

items.title: ServiceGroup
items.text:
Create services before the group. Like address groups, service groups accept names or named models as members. This example uses the custom services created above:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import ServiceGroup

services = ServiceGroup(name="example-application-services", member=[web, dns, "example-ping"])
fmg.add(services)

items.title: Virtual IPs
items.text: Use an open connection from the quickstart. Run the snippets on this page in order; write examples require unused names and valid references in your selected ADOM. Await requests when using an asynchronous client. See the firewall overview for firmware coverage and shared conventions.

items.title: VIP
items.text: VIP uses firewall/vip, with complete fields for static NAT, load balancing, SSL, real servers, GSLB, and QUIC from the reference. Array fields accept one value or a list. Address ranges and metadata-variable strings are preserved without imposing IP-only validation.

items.title: VIPDynamicMapping
items.text:
VIPDynamicMapping is a separate model because the mapping schema has different fields and types: for example, parent extintf is an array, mapping extintf is a string, and mapping real servers include seq. Pass a mapping object/dictionary or a list in dynamic_mapping; it is always serialized as an array. mapping__scope accepts a Scope, dictionary, or list and uses the API alias _scope on the wire.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import VIP, VIPDynamicMapping

vip = VIP(
    name="web", extintf="wan1", extip="203.0.113.10", mappedip="192.0.2.10",
    portforward="enable", extport="443", mappedport="8443",
    dynamic_mapping=VIPDynamicMapping(
        mapping__scope=Scope(name="FG01", vdom="root"),
        extintf="wan2", extip="203.0.113.20", mappedip="192.0.2.20",
    ),
)
fmg.add(vip)

Mappings are embedded in parent writes, as with existing address mappings. GET returns typed mapping rows. Use dynamic_mapping=[] in an update to send an empty mapping array; leaving it None omits the field. Separate mapping-endpoint CRUD wrappers are not provided.

items.title: Object guides
items.text:
Choose the domain that matches your task. These guides use the implemented Python models; the generated code reference provides their full field lists and docstrings.

Domain Classes and workflows Firewall objects Addresses, groups, services, security profile groups, proxy objects, VIPs, IP pools Devices and ADOMs ADOM, Device, VDOM, nested HASlave records Policies and packages PolicyPackage, PackageSettings, Policy Normalized interfaces NormalizedInterface, nested DynamicMapping and PlatformMapping Device system settings DeviceInterface, DeviceZone, SystemAdmin Device operations DeviceCommand, DeviceTask Tasks and installation Task, TaskLine, TaskLineHistory, InstallDeviceTask

items.title: Run the examples
items.text:
Configure a connection using the quickstart. Unless a context is shown, run request snippets inside with FMG(**config) as fmg:. With an asynchronous client, await requests, bound object operations, and task polling. Model construction and get_obj() remain synchronous.

Replace names with explicit targets in your selected ADOM. Read examples do not write configuration. Examples using ADD, UPDATE, SET, DELETE, or EXEC change state as described on their page. Constructing a model alone makes no API request. Referenced objects must already exist unless the example creates them.

The examples are checked locally against models and request construction. They were not run on a live device for this documentation update. Field availability depends on the target firmware and platform; model validation alone does not prove device compatibility.

items.title: Scope and coverage
items.text:
Device system models operate on FortiManager's managed-device configuration database. They do not establish a direct FortiGate connection. Saving database changes and installing them onto a FortiGate are separate operations.

Nested data models are not necessarily independent resources. Use them in their parent objects or inspect them in responses as documented. The pm_config_cli module is currently a placeholder and has no implemented high-level CLI-template classes.

items.title: Device operations
items.text: The dvmcmd module represents device-manager execution operations. Use these for managed-device lifecycle workflows, rather than assuming Device.add() or Device.delete() has equivalent semantics. Read the device inventory guide and task guide first.

items.title: DeviceCommand
items.text:
DeviceCommand extends the inventory model with command-specific fields, including device_action and device_blueprint. Constructing it makes no request:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmcmd import DeviceCommand

candidate = DeviceCommand(
    name="example-model-fw",
    sn="FGVMEXAMPLE000001",
    device_action="add_model",
)

This is an illustrative model-device definition. Replace the serial number and supply any additional platform or version fields required by your target firmware before execution. This documentation update does not establish a complete enrollment recipe for every firmware.

items.title: DeviceTask
items.text:
A DeviceTask takes an explicit ADOM and a Device or DeviceCommand instance. Deletion also accepts a device name string; adding requires the configuration in a device model. The action selects the add or delete command. Build an add request locally:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmcmd import DeviceTask

add_task = DeviceTask(
    adom=fmg.adom,
    device=candidate,
    action="add",
    flags=["create_task"],
)

Only execute the request after checking the target, prerequisites, and unused device identity:

response = fmg.exec(add_task)
state = response.wait_for_task()
if state != "done":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Device operation did not complete successfully: {state}")

Keep the connection open while polling. The response can indicate request acceptance before the device-manager operation completes.

For removal, construct a separate request using an explicitly named existing device:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmdb import Device

remove_task = DeviceTask(
    adom=fmg.adom,
    device=Device(name="retired-example-fw"),
    action="del",
    flags=["create_task"],
)

This snippet only constructs the removal request. Executing it removes the device from FortiManager and can have consequences beyond object cleanup. For deletion, a device model is converted to its name in the request payload; device="retired-example-fw" produces the same payload. Workspace discard does not provide a general undo for device lifecycle operations.

items.title: Devices and ADOMs
items.text: The dvmdb module models FortiManager's device inventory and administrative domains. Use the connection and scope conventions in the object guide.

items.title: ADOM
items.text:
Read the ADOM inventory or select an ADOM by name:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmdb import ADOM

adoms = fmg.get(ADOM).data
for adom in adoms:
    print(adom.name, adom.desc)

selected = fmg.get(ADOM(name="branch-adom")).first()
if selected is not None:
    print(selected.name, selected.workspace_mode)

ADOM inventory uses a system-wide route. Selecting fmg.adom does not restrict this inventory to that one ADOM; permissions still apply.

To change the description of an existing ADOM, target it explicitly:

fmg.update(ADOM(name="branch-adom", desc="Branch administration"))

ADOM creation, deletion, and cloning affect lifecycle state. The model exposes the corresponding object operations, but confirm the target and firmware requirements before using them. They are not made safe by choosing another ADOM in the connection settings.

items.title: Device
items.text:
Device describes a managed device in the selected ADOM. Use filters to choose a device, rather than taking the first device in an inventory:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import F
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmdb import Device

connected = fmg.get(Device, F(conn_status="up")).data
device = fmg.get(Device(name="branch-fw")).first()
if device is not None:
    print(device.name, device.hostname, device.conf_status)

To change inventory metadata for that existing device:

fmg.update(Device(name="branch-fw", desc="Branch edge firewall"))

For adding or removing a managed device, use the command objects in device operations. Do not assume generic configuration CRUD performs the same lifecycle workflow.

items.title: VDOM
items.text:
A VDOM lookup needs its parent device as well as the selected ADOM:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dvmdb import VDOM

vdoms = fmg.get(VDOM(device="branch-fw")).data
root_vdom = fmg.get(VDOM(device="branch-fw", name="root")).first()
for vdom in vdoms:
    print(vdom.name, vdom.comments)

device locates the parent and is excluded from the configuration payload. To obtain a mapping scope from an inventory record with loaded VDOMs:

device = fmg.get(Device(name="branch-fw")).first()
if device is not None and device.vdom:
    scope = device.get_vdom_scope("root")
    if scope is not None:
        print(scope.name, scope.vdom)

get_vdom_scope() uses the loaded device.vdom list; it does not fetch missing VDOM data. Handle absent VDOM data and a nonmatching VDOM explicitly.

items.title: HASlave
items.text:
HASlave represents nested HA member records returned in Device.ha_slave. It has no independent endpoint in the implementation. Inspect it through a device response:

device = fmg.get(Device(name="branch-fw")).first()
if device is not None:
    for member in device.ha_slave or []:
        print(member.name, member.role, member.status, member.conf_status)

A standalone fmg.get(HASlave) or write is not a supported workflow. Despite the historical class name, each record includes a role field that identifies its HA role.

items.title: Normalized interfaces
items.text: Normalized interfaces let policy configuration refer to a logical interface name rather than one physical interface on every device. The dynamic module models the parent and its mappings. Use an open connection as described in the object guide.

items.title: NormalizedInterface
items.text:
Read existing definitions or create a new definition with a default interface mapping:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dynamic import NormalizedInterface

interfaces = fmg.get(NormalizedInterface).data
for interface in interfaces:
    print(interface.name, interface.defmap_intf)

normalized = NormalizedInterface(
    name="example-lan",
    default_mapping="enable",
    defmap_intf="port1",
)
fmg.add(normalized)

The new name must be unused and the default mapping must be appropriate for the target devices. This creates FortiManager object configuration; it does not install a device interface.

wildcard, wildcard_intf, and zone_only are independent settings. wildcard and zone_only accept "enable" or "disable"; wildcard_intf holds the interface pattern. Python field names wildcard_intf and zone_only serialize as wildcard-intf and zone-only. API responses using the hyphenated names can be loaded directly:

normalized = NormalizedInterface.model_validate(
    {"name": "example-lan", "wildcard": "enable", "wildcard-intf": "port*", "zone-only": "disable"}
)
assert normalized.wildcard_intf == "port*"
assert normalized.zone_only == "disable"
payload = normalized.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)
assert payload["wildcard-intf"] == "port*"
assert payload["zone-only"] == "disable"

Fields omitted or set to None are excluded from write payloads. The former merged wildcard_intf_zone_only field is replaced by wildcard_intf and zone_only.

items.title: DynamicMapping
items.text:
DynamicMapping describes device/VDOM overrides nested in a normalized interface. Inspect returned entries through their parent:

parent = fmg.get(NormalizedInterface(name="example-lan")).first()
if parent is not None:
    mappings = parent.dynamic_mapping or []
    if not isinstance(mappings, list):
        mappings = [mappings]
    for mapping in mappings:
        print(mapping.mapping__scope, mapping.local_intf)

To construct an override locally:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dynamic import DynamicMapping

override = DynamicMapping(
    mapping__scope=Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root"),
    local_intf=["port2"],
)
draft = NormalizedInterface(name="example-lan", dynamic_mapping=[override])
payload = draft.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)
assert payload["dynamic_mapping"][0]["local-intf"] == ["port2"]

items.title: PlatformMapping
items.text:
PlatformMapping describes a platform-specific interface mapping. Construct or inspect it as nested parent data:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.dynamic import PlatformMapping

platform = PlatformMapping(name="FortiGate-VM64", intf_zone="port1")
draft = NormalizedInterface(name="example-platform-lan", platform_mapping=[platform])
payload = draft.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)
assert payload["platform_mapping"][0]["intf-zone"] == "port1"

Replace the platform identifier with one supported by your FortiManager. These mapping examples demonstrate local model construction and serialization, not verified mapping writes.

Both mapping classes support the clients' get_url(method=...) calling convention. Standalone requests require interface to identify the parent. A specific dynamic mapping additionally requires both dynamic_mapping_name and dynamic_mapping_vdom; a platform mapping can be selected with platform_mapping. Omitting these selectors addresses the mapping collection. These routes have offline URL coverage; confirm firmware behavior before submitting mapping changes.

items.title: Policies and packages
items.text: The policy module models policy packages (PPs) and the policies within them. Use an explicit ADOM and the connection conventions in the object guide.

items.title: PolicyPackage
items.text:
Read packages in the selected scope, or select an existing package by name:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.policy import PolicyPackage

packages = fmg.get(PolicyPackage).data
package = fmg.get(PolicyPackage(name="branch-policy")).first()
for item in packages:
    print(item.name, item.type)

The model's name field identifies a package; scope_member describes its assigned devices and VDOMs. Both scope_member and the API spelling "scope member" are accepted as input; API payloads use "scope member". An omitted member list remains absent, while [] is sent explicitly. Folder responses contain nested PolicyPackage instances in subobj.

items.title: Manage scope members
items.text:
Packages returned by fmg.get are bound to their connection and ADOM. Use their member methods to change assignments without writing the other package settings:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope

package = fmg.get(PolicyPackage(name="branch-policy")).first()
members = [Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")]
package.add_scope_members(members)
package.delete_scope_members(members)
package.set_scope_members(members)
package.update_scope_members(members)
package.unset_scope_members()
package.refresh()

These calls demonstrate separate operations: ADD adds members, DELETE removes the supplied members, SET replaces the member list, UPDATE sends a member-table update, and UNSET clears all assignments. Each call returns an operation response. Check its success value when raise_on_error is disabled. The local scope_member list is reloaded only by refresh(). Member dictionaries such as {"name": "branch-fw", "vdom": "root"} are also accepted.

With AsyncFMG, await each call, including get and refresh:

package = (await fmg.get(PolicyPackage(name="branch-policy"))).first()
await package.add_scope_members([Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")])
await package.refresh()

For a locally constructed package, pass fmg=fmg and optionally fmg_scope="my-adom". The member methods require a package name; use its full path (for example, name="folder/branch-policy") when it is inside a folder. The connection's selected ADOM is used unless the package already has a scope. Global scope is also supported.

items.title: PackageSettings
items.text:
PackageSettings is embedded in a policy package, not added independently. Its ssl_ssh_profile field is a list of profile names, serialized as "ssl-ssh-profile"; a single string is also accepted and converted to a one-item list. This example creates a new package assigned to an existing device and VDOM:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.policy import PackageSettings, PolicyPackage

package = PolicyPackage(
    name="example-branch-policy",
    scope_member=[Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")],
    package_settings=PackageSettings(fwpolicy_implicit_log="enable"),
)
fmg.add(package)

The package name must be unused. Assigning a package and creating its database record do not install it onto the device. InstallDeviceTask is for device settings; this library currently has no dedicated high-level policy-package installation task.

items.title: Policy
items.text:
Supply pkg to locate the package and policyid when selecting an individual policy. The connection supplies the ADOM unless the model has an explicit adom.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.policy import Policy

policies = fmg.get(Policy(pkg="branch-policy")).data
policy = fmg.get(Policy(pkg="branch-policy", policyid=10)).first()
for item in policies:
    print(item.policyid, item.name, item.action)

To update one field on an existing policy:

fmg.update(Policy(pkg="branch-policy", policyid=10, comments="Reviewed branch rule"))

pkg and adom locate the resource and are excluded from the configuration payload. Address and service references accept names or supported named firewall models. Supplying a referenced model does not create it.

Policy profile references, including diameter_filter_profile, av_profile, ips_sensor, application_list, and profile_group, are lists of profile names, matching the FMG schema. Single strings are accepted and normalized to one-item lists. None omits a profile field from write payloads; an explicit [] is sent as an empty array. profile_type remains the "single" / "group" selector.

rule = Policy(pkg="branch-policy", policyid=10, diameter_filter_profile=["example-diameter"])
assert rule.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)["diameter-filter-profile"] == ["example-diameter"]

The following constructs a local rule for inspection. It does not write the rule:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.firewall import Address, ServiceCustom

rule = Policy(
    pkg="branch-policy",
    name="Example application access",
    srcintf=["lan"],
    dstintf=["wan"],
    srcaddr=[Address(name="example-network")],
    dstaddr=["all"],
    service=[ServiceCustom(name="example-web")],
    action="accept",
    schedule=["always"],
    logtraffic="all",
)
payload = rule.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)
assert payload["srcaddr"] == ["example-network"]
assert payload["service"] == ["example-web"]
assert "pkg" not in payload

Before adding a rule, confirm that the package, interfaces, addresses, services, and schedule exist, and review the intended policy placement. This example does not claim automatic ordering or package installation.

items.title: Device system settings
items.text: The system models address configuration stored in FortiManager for a managed FortiGate. They use explicit device names rather than a direct connection to the FortiGate. See the object guide for connection conventions.

items.title: DeviceInterface
items.text:
Read interfaces for an explicitly named device:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.system import DeviceInterface

interfaces = fmg.get(DeviceInterface(device="branch-fw")).data
port = fmg.get(DeviceInterface(device="branch-fw", name="port1")).first()
for interface in interfaces:
    print(interface.name, interface.alias)

To update an existing interface alias in FortiManager's database:

fmg.update(DeviceInterface(device="branch-fw", name="port1", alias="Branch LAN"))

name identifies the interface. interface is a separate parent-interface reference, used for VLANs and similar relationships. device and fmg_interface are URL-only fields. A local VLAN definition illustrates that distinction:

vlan = DeviceInterface(
    device="branch-fw",
    name="example-vlan",
    type="vlan",
    interface="port1",
    vlanid=123,
    vdom="root",
    ip="192.0.2.1/24",
)

This definition is not submitted. Device/platform support and interface dependencies must be checked before adding it. See advanced usage for the schema source and compatibility limits.

items.title: DeviceZone
items.text:
Zones belong to a device and VDOM. Read the zone collection:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.system import DeviceZone

zones = fmg.get(DeviceZone(device="branch-fw", vdom="root")).data
for zone in zones:
    print(zone.name, zone.interface)

To create a new zone using existing interfaces:

zone = DeviceZone(
    device="branch-fw",
    vdom="root",
    name="example-zone",
    interface=["port2"],
    intrazone="deny",
)
fmg.add(zone)

Use an unused zone name and an interface eligible for membership in that VDOM. Interface model references are also accepted and converted to names. The parent device and VDOM are excluded from the configuration payload.

items.title: SystemAdmin
items.text:
SystemAdmin addresses administrator configuration on the managed device, not FortiManager's own administrator accounts. It can return sensitive configuration; print only the fields needed.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.system import SystemAdmin

admins = fmg.get(SystemAdmin(device="branch-fw")).data
for admin in admins:
    print(admin.name)

To update a comment on an explicitly selected existing account:

fmg.update(SystemAdmin(
    device="branch-fw",
    name="existing-automation-user",
    comments="Managed by the automation team",
))

Changes remain in FortiManager's device configuration database until an appropriate installation. Review pending device settings before installing; installation may include unrelated pending changes.

items.title: Tasks and installation
items.text: Task creation, polling, and inspection are distinct steps. Use an open connection as described in the object guide, and keep it open until an operation has finished.

items.title: InstallDeviceTask
items.text:
InstallDeviceTask installs device settings from FortiManager onto explicitly selected devices. It is not a policy-package installation wrapper. Review pending configuration before execution: installation may apply changes made outside your script.

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import Scope
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.securityconsole import InstallDeviceTask

install = fmg.get_obj(
    InstallDeviceTask,
    adom=fmg.adom,
    scope=[Scope(name="branch-fw", vdom="root")],
    flags=["auto_lock_ws"],
)
response = install.exec()
state = response.wait_for_task(callback=lambda percent, log: print(percent, log))
if state != "done":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Installation did not complete successfully: {state}")

The device and VDOM must exist. With an asynchronous client, await install.exec() and response.wait_for_task(). A successful execution response does not establish successful installation. Missing task metadata or an unsuccessful status read can produce None; other terminal states also need application handling.

items.title: Task
items.text:
Task represents task status returned by FortiManager. Read it by filtering the collection:

from pyfortinet.fmg_api.common import F
from pyfortinet.fmg_api.task import Task

task = fmg.get(Task, F(id=123)).first()
if task is not None:
    print(task.id, task.state, task.percent, task.num_err)

Replace 123 with a task ID returned by an actual operation. The model has required response fields, so Task(id=123) is not a minimal lookup model; use the class and an F filter.

If the ID is already available, polling also works directly:

state = fmg.wait_for_task(123)

The low-level clients support this polling helper too. See advanced usage for callback and failure behavior.

items.title: TaskLine and TaskLineHistory
items.text:
TaskLine and TaskLineHistory describe nested task details. They do not define independent resource URLs. Inspect them through a Task response:

if task is not None:
    for line in task.line or []:
